newsitem.title: USA: Growth slowing but inflation risks remain - Rivlin.
newsitem.headline: Growth slowing but inflation risks remain - Rivlin.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The economy is slowing down from its exuberant first quarter pace, but still faces the risk of higher inflation down the road, Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said on Monday.
"We certainly have clearer signs that the economy is slowing, but we still have a tight labor market," she told Reuters in an interview.
That means that the central bank will again face a "tough call" next month in deciding whether to raise interest rates further, she said.
"If the Fed believes that inflation is a serious risk, then it should, in the interests of sustaining growth, tighten," Rivlin said. "It's just at the moment that's not crystal clear."
After increasing rates in March to keep the economy from overheating and to head off inflation, the Fed held policy steady at its last meeting in May amid hopes growth would slow.
The central bank next meets to plot monetary strategy on July 1-2 and Wall Street analysts are betting it will once again opt to keep rates unchanged.
Rivlin said that she did not think that the economic picture has changed all that much over the last few months.

While growth is slowing, it is not certain whether it is slowing enough to contain inflation or how long the slowdown will last, she said. And labor markets remain "very tight," raising the risk of big wage hikes and higher inflation.
"We still have these two things going on at once," Rivlin said. "We have an economy which is really slowing and we still have inflation risk. It could be that way for months."
Rivlin confessed that the current economic situation was "quite mystifying" but nevertheless welcome.
At 4.8 percent, the U.S. unemployment rate is at levels that in the past have led to stepped-up wage increases and higher inflation. But that has not happened this time.
"We have an inflation risk without inflation," she said.
She noted that many companies continue to report having trouble raising prices because of stiff competition from domestic and foreign rivals.
Besides the tight labor market, Rivlin pointed to the ebullient stock market as another area of possible concern.
"You have to be quite optimistic about (corporate) earnings to justify these kinds of (share) prices," she said. But she noted, "Earnings have been doing quite well."
With stock prices so high, there is a risk investors will respond by sharply stepping up their purchases of consumer goods, spurring growth too much and fanning inflation.
"We haven't actually seen that," Rivlin said. But that could still occur in the future, she added.
The Fed policymaker was generally upbeat about the longer-term economic outlook and saw no reason to worry about the economy falling into recession.
Although retail sales have ebbed in recent months, consumer confidence is very strong, personal incomes are rising and employment is high, she said.
"It looks like a very strong economy," Rivlin said. "The main risk is inflation."
